title: Venezuela’s Overwhelming Electricity Crisis
gist: Venezuela is suffering its worst blackout wave since 2019, and the article argues the country's post-Maduro-era economic recovery hinges on converting MOUs with GE Vernova and IMPSA into funded repair contracts, passing a private-investment electricity reform bill, and surviving a forecast severe El Niño that threatens 90%-hydro-dependent generation.

insights.claim: Venezuela is enduring its most intense wave of blackouts since 2019, with Acting President Delcy Rodríguez calling for water and electricity rationing amid rising social tension over the outages.
insights.speaker: FRANCISCO MORANDI AND LUISA PALACIOS
insights.so_what: Rising social unrest over power cuts raises political-stability risk in Venezuela just as the country attempts an economic recovery, a factor relevant to any Venezuela-exposed credit, equity, or commodity position.
insights.quote: the timing could not be worse for a country attempting a full-scale economic recovery

insights.claim: Blackouts that were previously confined to non-major urban centers have spread nationwide, with anecdotal daily blackouts of five to seven hours in Valencia (Venezuela's former manufacturing hub) and nearby Maracay, and companies reporting an average of 57 unplanned outages (about five per week) in Q2 2026.
insights.speaker: FRANCISCO MORANDI AND LUISA PALACIOS
insights.so_what: Repeated outages at this frequency directly impair industrial output in Venezuela's manufacturing base, a leading indicator for any non-oil recovery narrative.
insights.quote: companies reported an average of 57 unplanned outages, five a week, in the second quarter of the year
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "While Venezuelans from non-major urban centers"

insights.claim: New Venezuelan oil regulations now require oil companies expanding operations to supply their own electricity for related projects, because the public generation and distribution network is too degraded to rely on.
insights.speaker: FRANCISCO MORANDI AND LUISA PALACIOS
insights.so_what: Oil operators entering or expanding in Venezuela must now budget for captive power generation as a cost of doing business, raising the capital intensity of new oil projects.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "While Venezuelans from non-major urban centers"

themes.theme: Foreign repair contracts as the near-term fix

insights.claim: State-owned Corpoelec and GE Vernova signed an MOU to repair, modernize, and stabilize Venezuela's electricity system, targeting roughly 1,000 megawatts of restored generating capacity within 24 months and more than 5,000 megawatts over four to five years.
insights.speaker: FRANCISCO MORANDI AND LUISA PALACIOS
insights.so_what: A funded, executed version of this MOU is the single largest identifiable near-term catalyst for Venezuelan grid capacity; watch whether the MOU converts into a signed final contract.
insights.quote: restore roughly 1,000 megawatts of generating capacity within 24 months and more than 5,000 megawatts over four to five years
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Earlier this year, the state-owned Corpoelec"

insights.claim: GE Vernova CEO Scott Strazik indicated the Corpoelec partnership would extend to rehabilitating the 11 gigawatts of installed generating capacity GE already has in Venezuela, far larger in scope than the initial MOU targets.
insights.speaker: FRANCISCO MORANDI AND LUISA PALACIOS
insights.so_what: If realized, GE Vernova stands to become the dominant foreign player rebuilding Venezuelan power infrastructure, a multi-year revenue opportunity contingent on the political/payment framework being resolved.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Earlier this year, the state-owned Corpoelec"

insights.claim: U.S.-Argentine company IMPSA signed a separate accord with Corpoelec to rehabilitate and complete two long-stalled hydroelectric projects, Tocoma and Macagua in Bolívar state, targeting 672 megawatts of restored capacity within 24 months.
insights.speaker: FRANCISCO MORANDI AND LUISA PALACIOS
insights.so_what: Tocoma and Macagua completion would meaningfully add to hydro capacity right as El Niño threatens hydro output, making IMPSA's execution timeline a key variable to track.

insights.claim: Two critical decisions were postponed by the June earthquakes and remain unresolved: signing a final (not just MOU-stage) contract with GE Vernova, and scheduling a final legislative vote on the electricity reform bill — both are now the key near-term catalysts to watch.
insights.speaker: FRANCISCO MORANDI AND LUISA PALACIOS
insights.so_what: Until these two items move, the repair effort remains at the MOU/proposal stage rather than funded execution — a binary catalyst pair for anyone tracking Venezuela's power-sector turnaround.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Executing two critical decisions postponed"

insights.claim: Unresolved arrears and uncertainty over securing future payments to foreign suppliers such as GE Vernova and Siemens Energy remain the key sticking points slowing the pace of infrastructure repair.
insights.speaker: FRANCISCO MORANDI AND LUISA PALACIOS
insights.so_what: Payment/sanctions-related friction, not technical capacity, is the binding constraint on Venezuela's grid repair — a signal that sanctions relief or payment-guarantee mechanisms matter more than engineering timelines.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Engaging foreign companies such as GE Vernova"

themes.theme: El Niño as a coming stress test

insights.claim: Recent forecasts put the probability of a very strong El Niño event from October to December 2026 at 90%, a major threat because hydroelectricity supplies 90% of Venezuela's power and its thermal fleet is largely unavailable or unreliable as backup.
insights.speaker: FRANCISCO MORANDI AND LUISA PALACIOS
insights.so_what: A near-certain severe El Niño against a grid with almost no thermal backup makes Q4 2026 a high-probability window for a sharp deterioration in Venezuelan power supply and associated social/political risk.
insights.quote: there is a 90 % chance of a very strong El Niño from October to December this year
insights.locator: section "El Niño: the next major stress test"

insights.claim: Under a worst-case El Niño drought scenario, water pumping, agriculture, and fuel logistics would be hit, and eastern Venezuelan oil production — which is more grid-dependent than western production — could also be impaired.
insights.speaker: FRANCISCO MORANDI AND LUISA PALACIOS
insights.so_what: A severe El Niño is a plausible near-term downside catalyst for Venezuelan oil output specifically in the eastern fields, worth flagging for any oil-supply forecast that assumes steady Venezuelan production.
insights.locator: section "El Niño: the next major stress test"

insights.claim: Adding new thermal generation capacity for oil production is constrained by backlogs of up to five years for natural gas turbines, a shortage the authors attribute partly to competing demand from the U.S. data center build-out.
insights.speaker: FRANCISCO MORANDI AND LUISA PALACIOS
insights.so_what: Global AI/data-center demand for gas turbines is crowding out equipment availability for emerging-market power buildouts like Venezuela's, a cross-sector supply-chain link worth tracking for turbine-OEM order books (GE Vernova, Siemens Energy) and for any country relying on gas-fired backup power.
insights.locator: section "El Niño: the next major stress test", closing paragraph

themes.theme: Electricity reform: investment opening with structural deterrents

insights.claim: Venezuela's electricity reform bill would open generation, transmission, and distribution to private participation through single and joint companies with the state, via concessions of up to 25 years with possible extensions, and allow projects under 2 megawatts of capacity to proceed without a government permit.
insights.speaker: FRANCISCO MORANDI AND LUISA PALACIOS
insights.so_what: The sub-2MW permit-free threshold is a specific, actionable detail for any company or investor considering self-generation/distributed power projects in Venezuela ahead of the bill's passage.
insights.locator: section "The electricity reform: advantages and drawbacks"

insights.claim: The reform's concessions revert fully to the state at the end of the license term (a build-operate-transfer structure), with significant uncertainty about how compensation will be handled and broad state discretion over grounds for cancellation — a structural deterrent to long-horizon private capital.
insights.speaker: FRANCISCO MORANDI AND LUISA PALACIOS
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating Venezuelan power concessions should price in expropriation-adjacent terminal risk and discretionary cancellation risk, not just headline concession length.
insights.quote: the concessions revert to the state at the end of the license
insights.locator: section "The electricity reform: advantages and drawbacks"

insights.claim: The bill also grants the government significant discretionary oversight and penalty power, including civil and even criminal liability for executives and directors across a wide range of issues — a serious risk given Venezuela's weak rule-of-law environment.
insights.speaker: FRANCISCO MORANDI AND LUISA PALACIOS
insights.so_what: Personal criminal liability exposure for executives is a concrete deterrent that could keep multinational power operators on the sidelines even if commercial terms improve.
insights.locator: section "The electricity reform: advantages and drawbacks"

insights.claim: The authors' framework for the reform succeeding: it will only unlock meaningful investment if paired with bankable contracts, transparent project selection, cost-reflective tariffs, payment security, credible dispute-resolution mechanisms, rule-of-law improvements, and multilateral support — absent these, private capital will flow only into self-generation, a suboptimal outcome for the wider grid.
insights.speaker: FRANCISCO MORANDI AND LUISA PALACIOS
insights.so_what: This is a concrete checklist investors and multilaterals can use to judge whether Venezuela's reform is investment-grade in practice versus merely on paper.
insights.quote: Without these conditions, private capital may flow only to self-generation opportunities, leading to suboptimal solutions.
insights.locator: section "The electricity reform: advantages and drawbacks", closing paragraph

themes.theme: Outlook: electricity as the recovery bottleneck

insights.claim: The authors frame Venezuela's electricity sector as facing four simultaneous challenges — converting MOUs into funded contracts, repairing earthquake-damaged infrastructure, finalizing the private-investment legal framework, and preparing for a climate shock that could cut hydropower — and argue that mastering all four together is the central test of the country's capacity to recover.
insights.speaker: FRANCISCO MORANDI AND LUISA PALACIOS
insights.so_what: Electricity capacity, not oil output alone, is positioned as the key leading indicator for Venezuela's broader post-Maduro economic recovery trajectory.
insights.quote: they make electricity the central test of the country’s capacity to recover
